title: JVM Memory Model & Garbage Collection
prompt: Explain the JVM memory model: heap, stack, and Metaspace. How does garbage collection work, and why was Metaspace introduced in Java 8?
hints: Split your answer into three regions: heap, JVM stack, and Metaspace — what lives in each?
Mention that heap objects are collected by GC generations (young vs old), while stack frames are freed on method return.
Recall that pre-Java 8 permanent generation (PermGen) had a fixed size, which Metaspace replaces with native memory.
Name a concrete GC algorithm, e.g., G1, and when it runs (minor/major/full GC).
idealAnswer: The JVM divides memory into several runtime areas. The heap is the shared region where all class instances and arrays are allocated; it is managed by the garbage collector and is typically split into young generation (Eden + survivor spaces) and old generation (tenured). The JVM stack is per-thread and holds frames containing local variables, partial results, and references; a frame is pushed on method call and popped on return, so stack memory is freed deterministically. Metaspace (Java 8+) stores class metadata and static fields that were previously in the permanent generation (PermGen); unlike PermGen it resides in native memory and grows by default, reducing OutOfMemoryError risks caused by fixed class metadata limits. Garbage collection reclaims unreachable objects. Most collectors are generational and tracing-based (e.g., G1): objects start in Eden, survive in survivor spaces after minor GCs, and get promoted to the old generation; when the old generation fills, a major/full GC runs. Modern collectors like G1 and ZGC aim for low, predictable pause times and reclaim large portions of the heap concurrently with application threads.
keyPoints: Heap = objects/arrays, shared, GC-managed, generational (young + old).
Stack = per-thread frames with locals; freed on method return.
Metaspace = class metadata in native memory, replaces PermGen, auto-grows.
GC is tracing/generational: minor GC on young gen, major/full GC on old gen; G1/ZGC pursue low pauses.

title: String Immutability & String vs StringBuilder
prompt: Why are Strings immutable in Java, and what are the practical differences between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer?
hints: Think about why immutability helps with thread safety, caching, and the string pool.
Remember that String concatenation in a loop creates many intermediate objects — mention that.
StringBuilder vs StringBuffer: the difference is synchronization.
Mention Java 17+ features like text blocks and the compact strings storage optimization.
idealAnswer: String objects are immutable: once created, their char sequence cannot change (the internal byte/char array is final and not exposed). This gives several benefits: immutability makes Strings naturally thread-safe, allows them to be safely cached (hashCode is computed once and reused), and enables the string pool — literals are interned so equal strings share one instance, saving memory. Immutability also makes Strings safe as hash map keys because their hashCode never changes. The downside is that repeated concatenation, e.g., in a loop, creates a new String per iteration, which is inefficient. StringBuilder is a mutable char sequence with no synchronization, making it the fastest choice for building strings in single-threaded code; StringBuffer is identical in API but synchronizes its methods, so it is thread-safe yet slower. Since Java 9+, Strings are stored as bytes (LATIN-1 or UTF-16) with a coder flag, so ASCII-only strings use half the memory. Java 15+ text blocks make multiline string literals much more readable.
keyPoints: Strings are immutable -> thread-safe, hash-safe, poolable.
Concatenation in loops is inefficient; use StringBuilder.
StringBuilder = unsynchronized/fast; StringBuffer = synchronized/slow.
Java 9+ compact strings store as bytes; text blocks improve multiline literals.

title: equals/hashCode Contract
prompt: Explain the equals() and hashCode() contract in Java. Why must they be consistent, and what happens if you override one but not the other?
hints: State the three properties of equals: reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, plus consistency and non-null.
The contract with hashCode: equal objects must have equal hash codes.
Think of HashMap/HashSet: they use hashCode to find the bucket, equals to confirm the match.
Consider what breaks when hashCode is omitted — lookup failures.
Java 17: hashCode of a record is derived automatically from components.
idealAnswer: The equals(Object) contract requires reflexivity (x.equals(x) is true), symmetry, transitivity, consistency (repeated calls give the same result for unchanged objects), and that x.equals(null) is false. The hashCode() contract states that two objects that are equal per equals() must produce the same hash code; unequal objects may share a hash code, but fewer collisions improve hash-table performance. These two methods are tightly coupled because collections like HashMap and HashSet rely on hashCode to locate the bucket and equals to resolve collisions. If you override equals but not hashCode, two equal objects can land in different buckets, so contains()/get() fail even though equality holds — a classic bug. Overriding hashCode without equals breaks the mathematical equality that the contract requires and lets distinct objects be treated as duplicates. Practical guidance: always override both together, use Objects.equals() and Objects.hash() (or Java 7+ Arrays helper) to avoid null handling, and prefer final fields so the hash code is stable. Since Java 16, records auto-generate equals and hashCode from components, eliminating this error-prone boilerplate for data carriers.
keyPoints: equals: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, null-safe.
Equal objects must share a hashCode (the core contract).
HashMap buckets = hashCode; collision resolution = equals.
Override both together or use records to get them for free.

title: Java Streams & Functional Programming
prompt: Describe the Stream API in Java. What are intermediate vs terminal operations, and how does functional-style processing differ from traditional loops?
hints: Distinguish intermediate (lazy, return a stream) from terminal (eager, produce a result) operations.
Mention common ones: map, filter, flatMap, sorted vs collect, reduce, forEach.
Laziness matters: intermediate ops don't execute until a terminal op runs.
Mention parallel streams, orElse vs orElseGet, and Collectors.toList()/groupingBy() as modern idiom.
idealAnswer: Streams are a lazy sequence abstraction over a data source, enabling declarative, functional-style processing. The pipeline has three parts: a source (collection, array, stream factory), zero or more intermediate operations, and exactly one terminal operation. Intermediate operations such as map, filter, flatMap, sorted, and distinct are lazy — they return a new stream and do no work until a terminal operation is invoked. Terminal operations such as collect, reduce, forEach, count, and anyMatch are eager and produce a result or side effect; only they trigger the whole pipeline. Compared to an imperative loop with an accumulator variable, streams express intent more readably (filter + map + collect instead of nested loops and mutable temp lists), compose naturally, and can be parallelized by simply calling parallel(). Key idioms include Collectors.toList(), Collectors.groupingBy(), Collectors.toMap(), and Optional chaining for null-safe results (orElse, orElseGet, map on Optional). Common pitfalls: reusing a consumed stream (IllegalStateException), forgetting that intermediate ops are lazy so nothing runs without a terminal op, and performance overhead when boxing or iterating tiny datasets. Java 17 adds Stream.toList() and Stream.mapMulti, making common pipelines shorter.
keyPoints: Intermediate ops are lazy; terminal ops trigger execution.
Composition replaces loops/accumulators -> more declarative and testable.
parallel() gives easy parallelism; collect/toList finishes pipelines.
Pitfalls: consumed streams, laziness surprises, boxing overhead.

title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
prompt: Explain the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java. When should you use each, and how does try-with-resources simplify resource handling?
hints: Checked exceptions extend Exception (not RuntimeException) and must be declared or caught at compile time.
Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException (and Error) and are not enforced by the compiler.
IOException, SQLException are checked; NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ArithmeticException are unchecked.
Mention try-with-resources (Java 7+) for AutoCloseable and that a finally block can still be added.
Java 17: multi-catch and the var keyword; think about when throwing checked exceptions is appropriate.
idealAnswer: Checked exceptions extend Exception but not RuntimeException; the compiler forces callers to handle them — either with a try/catch or by declaring them in the method signature with throws. They represent recoverable, anticipated conditions outside normal program flow, such as IOException when reading a file or SQLException on a bad query. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException (or Error) and need no declaration or catch: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, and ArithmeticException (division by zero) are examples. They usually indicate programming bugs or conditions that are not reasonably recoverable. Good practice: use checked exceptions for external, expected failures where the caller can meaningfully react; use unchecked exceptions for contract violations and defects. Over-using checked exceptions leads to verbose code; modern guidance favors unchecked exceptions plus clear documentation, with Optional as an alternative to null-returning methods. Since Java 7, try-with-resources automatically closes AutoCloseable resources, guaranteeing release of files, sockets, and JDBC connections even when an exception is thrown; you can add catch and finally blocks as usual. Java 17 also supports multi-catch (catch (IOException | SQLException e)) to handle multiple related checked exceptions without duplication.
keyPoints: Checked: must be caught/declared; for recoverable external failures (IO, SQL).
Unchecked (RuntimeException): not enforced; for programming bugs.
Prefer unchecked for contract violations; Optional to avoid nulls.
try-with-resources auto-closes AutoCloseable resources reliably.
